title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) to measure whether inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM intent→configuration generator and an emulated execution reduces the proportion of configurations that would execute with operational faults. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics (one identical LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification), we evaluated 72 preregistered paired intents with gpt-5-mini and a canonical deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed with 144 episodes (72 pairs) and 72 model calls. All baseline executions produced no emulator-observed faults (n_11 = 72; n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected-fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract this degenerate confirmatory outcome is expected when identical generated candidates produce no baseline execution faults. We present the preregistration rationale, deterministic execution accounting, representative validator diagnostics, exact inferential outputs, and artifact-grounded recommendations for follow-on confirmatory designs able to detect verifier utility under realistic baseline-error regimes.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate high-level operator intents into device-level network configurations. This intent→configuration automation can speed change pipelines but risks silently violating reachability, access-control, ordering, or workflow invariants and thereby causing outages if generated text is executed without additional checks. A standard operational mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that combines stochastic LLM generation with deterministic verification and, if needed, repair or human review. Despite many architectural proposals and prototypes, systematic preregistered experiments that measure a verifier's detection performance against executed outcomes under tightly controlled paired designs remain scarce.

This paper answers a narrowly scoped, preregistered research question: does inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM generator and emulator execution materially reduce the proportion of configurations that execute with operational faults when the identical generated candidate is evaluated both without and with verification? That estimand isolates verifier detection from improvements that could arise from re-sampling, prompt-engineering, or repair-enabled iterations. We executed study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 across 72 preregistered paired intents under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The run completed with no technical failures and produced a degenerate confirmatory outcome (no baseline emulator faults). Rather than treating this as a null failure, we analyze why it occurred given the preregistered contract and archived artifacts, and we provide concrete, artifact-grounded guidance for designs that can detect verifier utility when baseline error prevalence is non-negligible.
sections.related_work:
Prior work establishes three pertinent points relevant to our inquiry. First, LLMs can produce plausible device-level configurations from high-level intent in constrained vendor-dialect settings and curated evaluation suites; such empirical demonstrations motivate intent→configuration automation but stop short of production-scale safety claims [1]. Second, multi-agent and tool‑augmented frameworks integrate verifiers, retrieval, and domain services into NetOps workflows to reduce regressions; production reports and prototypes illustrate feasible integration points but do not provide preregistered paired measurements of verifier detection against executed faults [2]. Third, generate–verify–repair (GVR) patterns are proposed and empirically instantiated in code and software-repair domains, where deterministic verification can convert stochastic generation into a correctness-convergent workflow; these studies show that verifier utility depends strongly on baseline generator error rates and on whether the pipeline permits verifier-triggered repair or resampling [3].

Canonical deterministic network verification techniques (e.g., header-space analysis and incremental policy checkers) provide precise invariants for reachability and ACL-style checks and are natural candidates for the verify stage, but the literature lacks preregistered paired experiments that measure how often such verifiers would detect faults that would otherwise manifest when LLM-generated configurations are executed in an emulator [4]. Our experiment directly targets that measurement gap using a preregistered paired design and deterministic accounting.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 before observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational-fault proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The confirmatory hypothesis (H1) targeted an absolute paired reduction of 0.20 (two-sided α = 0.05, power ≥ 0.80); a heuristic power calculation yielded ≈63 pairs and we preregistered N = 72 pairs stratified equally across three topology/difficulty strata.

Shared_initial_candidate contract. The execution contract enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent we performed a single LLM generation and evaluated that identical candidate in two paired conditions. Baseline: execute the shared candidate in an isolated emulator and record whether emulator-observed operational faults occur. Guarded: run the deterministic verifier on the same candidate; if the verifier flags violations the guarded outcome is recorded as prevented (no executed fault); otherwise execute the identical candidate in the emulator and record the outcome. Under this design any observed paired difference can only arise from the verifier preventing execution of a candidate that would otherwise have failed at emulation.

Model and verifier configuration (archived). The declared model is gpt-5-mini; key recorded model parameters included declared_model_version="gpt-5-mini", provider="openai_responses", max_output_tokens=2000, and maximum_attempts_per_call=1. The recorded temperature field is null; this indicates provider-default runtime sampling semantics were used (i.e., sampling parameters were not explicitly set to a numeric temperature) and should not be interpreted as evidence of deterministic temperature=0 sampling. The canonical verifier used is deterministic_netops_validator_v5, configured to run the full_intent_constraint_validation rule set; the verifier emits a structured trace per episode documenting parsed/required command counts, normalized configuration, validation_before/after states, violation codes, and violation_count. The verifier's binary validity verdict and trace for each episode were archived and used to determine guarded outcomes.

Task construction and contamination controls. Confirmatory tasks were generated deterministically by a task generator that encodes: a natural-language intent, a machine-structured required_sequence (ordered field changes), allowed_touched_fields, preserved-state policies, initial and expected_final_state snapshots, and a difficulty.level tag (medium/hard/very_hard). The preregistration required exact-match contamination checks against public corpora; exact-match contaminated items are excluded (none were excluded in this run). The confirmatory sample followed the preregistered stratification (24 pairs per stratum).

Execution, retries, and deterministic accounting. The missingness plan permitted up to two retries for transient API errors. The run completed without technical failures. Deterministic accounting reported: planned_episode_count = 144; completed_episode_count = 144; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 72 (one shared generation per pair). Provider-call audit confirmed 72 completed hosted-model call events and stage_counts consistent with a single shared_initial_generation per pair. All provider events and retries were logged in archived manifests.

Scoring and analysis. The verifier applied the full_intent_constraint_validation rule set to each shared candidate; per-episode validator traces determine whether a candidate was flagged. The primary analysis used a preregistered paired-binary analysis executor (McNemar-style exact test when discordant pairs exist) and a paired bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Pre-specified subgroup comparisons and sensitivity analyses (e.g., treating excluded pairs as failures) were implemented in the deterministic analysis pipeline and archived. Because no discordant pairs occurred the primary inferential outcome is degenerate but numerically exact and reproducible from archived artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution summary. The autonomous pipeline completed without technical failures. Key manifest figures: planned_episode_count = 144; completed_episode_count = 144; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 72; artifact_count = 510. Condition summaries show baseline successes = 72, baseline failures = 0 (success_rate = 1.0) and guarded successes = 72, guarded failures = 0 (success_rate = 1.0).

Paired contingency and inference. Aggregating across 72 confirmatory pairs produced contingency counts n_11 = 72, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 (guarded × baseline). The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline undetected-fault proportion) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) is [0.0, 0.0]. These tabulations are recorded in the archived paired contingency and condition summary artifacts.

Representative validator diagnostics. Representative per-episode validator traces show that generated candidates matched task-manifest constraints and were accepted by the verifier: examples include tasks with difficulty.level = "medium" (parsed_command_count = required_command_count = 4, violation_count = 0) and tasks labeled "hard" (parsed_command_count equals required_command_count, violation_count = 0). Across the confirmatory set the verifier did not flag violations and no automated repair was applied. Contamination and missingness summaries report zero exact-match contaminations and zero failed/unscorable episodes.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation. Under the shared_initial_candidate contract the estimand measures only whether a verifier can prevent execution of an identical candidate that would otherwise have failed in the emulator. Because the identical generated candidates produced zero emulator-observed faults there was no room for the verifier to demonstrate a reduction in executed faults; the degenerate numerical outcome (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0) follows directly from the preregistered design and observed data. This is an expected algebraic consequence of the estimand rather than a paradoxical failure of analysis.

Diagnostic attribution. Archived artifacts permit concrete attribution of this ceiling outcome to aligned design factors: (i) the deterministic task generator encoded explicit required_sequence and allowed_touched_fields that constrain correct solutions; (ii) the model (gpt-5-mini) produced candidates that closely matched those constraints for the synthetic corpus; and (iii) the verifier enforced the same task-manifest constraints. This alignment—constrained intents, congruent verifier rules, and matching generations—explains the absence of baseline emulator faults.

Design implications and recommendations. To measure verifier utility in a non-degenerate way, confirmatory designs should ensure a measurable baseline fault prevalence or allow verifier-mediated interventions. Preregistered alternatives include: (a) independent-generation arms (separate initial samples per condition) so verifier-triggered repair or sampling can change candidate distributions; (b) repair-enabled flows that permit a single deterministic repair call when the verifier flags a violation and then measure execution outcomes of repaired candidates; (c) adversarial or ambiguity-seeded task banks to raise baseline error rates; (d) sampling-parameter sweeps and multi-model comparisons; and (e) explicit false-positive cost arms to quantify operational blocking. All of these alternatives are preregisterable and implementable within the same deterministic execution and analysis infrastructure archived with this study.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolates verifier detection and was enforced by provider-call accounting. Construct validity: emulator-executed faults are a conservative surrogate for operational harm but do not capture traffic-dependent timing or vendor-hardware idiosyncrasies. External validity: the run used a single declared model and a synthetic task bank; extrapolation to other models, richer real-world distributions, or production hardware is limited. Conclusion validity: with zero baseline faults the preregistered power target (absolute 0.20 reduction) is moot; future confirmatory designs must align expected baseline prevalence with power targets.

Operational implication. The observed ceiling outcome does not imply verifiers are unnecessary. Instead, it documents a reproducible case where constrained intents, congruent verifier rules, and a capable LLM produced device-level sequences that both passed deterministic checks and emulator execution. Measuring the verifier's operational value in practice requires designs that produce a non-negligible baseline error rate or that permit verifier-driven corrections.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation (c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) under shared_initial_candidate semantics to test whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM-generated configurations that would execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and synthetic/emulated task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator faults and the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference = 0.0; bootstrap 95% CI [0.0,0.0]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). This artifact-grounded null/ceiling outcome is internally consistent with the preregistered design: when identical generated candidates produce no executed faults a verifier cannot reduce executed faults under the shared_initial_candidate contract. Measuring verifier utility under realistic error regimes requires preregistered contracts that permit independent or multiple generator samples, repair-enabled flows, adversarial task sets, and multi-model comparisons. The archived artifacts and deterministic accounting provide a reproducible template for such follow-on, powered confirmatory designs.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock. Human role: a Research Director selected the topic family and approved the immutable initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; no human manually edited technical manuscript content after the lock. Models and orchestration: initial generation used gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model configuration) orchestrated via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 served as the canonical verifier; an isolated emulator executed candidate configurations. Preregistration: study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 was preregistered and frozen before observing outcomes. Immutable master-prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Key archived artifacts (manifests, per-episode verifier traces, and analysis outputs) are retained in the execution and analysis archives associated with the preregistration.
limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: the baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per-condition generation, multi-sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single-model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling-parameter uncertainty: the model configuration records temperature = null (sampling parameters unset); null indicates provider-default runtime sampling semantics and is a residual uncertainty recorded in the archived configuration.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact-match checks were applied, but private training-data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
